pages.x: The East India Company ruled much of India with an army of Indian soldiers, called sepoys. Anger had been growing over kingdoms taken over, taxes and missionaries. Then came a new rifle whose paper cartridges, the soldiers heard, were greased with cow and pig fat and had to be bitten open: an insult to Hindus and Muslims alike.

In March 1857, at Barrackpore near Calcutta, a sepoy named Mangal Pandey attacked his British officers. He was hanged, and his regiment was broken up. The British called the rebels pandies after him; to Indians today he is one of the first heroes of the struggle for freedom.

In May, at Meerut, 85 soldiers who had refused the cartridges were chained and jailed. The next evening their comrades rose, freed them, killed British officers and civilians, and rode through the night to Delhi. There they proclaimed the old Mughal emperor, Bahadur Shah Zafar, ruler of India once more.

The revolt spread across the north, to Lucknow, Kanpur and Jhansi, joined by princes who had lost their lands and peasants with grievances of their own. Both sides killed without mercy. At Kanpur British women and children were massacred after the garrison surrendered, and British columns took revenge by hanging and burning whole villages.

In September, after a long siege, British and loyal Indian troops, many of them Sikhs and Gurkhas, stormed Delhi street by street. Bahadur Shah Zafar, a poet of 82, was caught and sent into exile in Burma, and his sons were shot. In Lucknow the besieged British residency held out for months until it was relieved.

Lakshmibai, the young widowed queen of Jhansi, whose kingdom the Company had taken because she had no son of her own, became the rising's most famous leader. When the British stormed Jhansi in 1858 she escaped, the story goes, with her adopted son tied to her back. She was killed fighting near Gwalior, dressed as a cavalry soldier.

In 1858 Parliament ended the East India Company's rule, and India passed to the British Crown, governed by a viceroy for Queen Victoria, who later took the title Empress of India. The Mughal Empire was ended for good, and the British promised not to meddle with Indian religions or take more princes' lands.

Many thousands died on both sides, and the bitterness lasted. The British ruled more warily afterwards, leaning on princes and landlords. For Indian nationalists the rising became the First War of Independence, and its heroes, like the Rani of Jhansi, inspired the movement that won India its freedom in 1947.
